progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: b11 (selective toxicity: a useful drug harms the pathogen much more than the host, often by hitting a part the pathogen has and we lack; the cell wall and ribosome targets; kill against stop-growth; resistance is selected; effectiveness is judged from clinical evidence); p02 (agar plates, aseptic technique, spreading 0.1 mL with a sterile spreader, label the base, tape with two strips, incubate upside down at 25 to 30 °C, never 37 °C, never opened, autoclave; risk group 1; VRA cards); s07 (in Biology after p02: validity, reliability, accuracy as three questions; word, feature, fix; repeats help reliability). Year 11 Module 2 (diffusion: net movement from high to low concentration). Not assumed: zone of inhibition, disc diffusion, breakpoints.
progression.startsWith: Set up safe controlled agar comparisons. The video opens: A student put four paper discs on a plate spread with bacteria. Two days later, around disc A, a clear zone twenty five millimetres across. Around disc B, fifteen.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining how a zone of inhibition forms; stating the aim, variables, negative control and replicates; preparing a lawn and placing discs; recalling safe incubation; measuring zones through the base; reading the results and judging reliability; explaining what zone size depends on; explaining why a zone does not show clinical effectiveness; judging validity, reliability and accuracy; writing the risk assessment; assessing a treatment claim from zone data and fixing a flawed method.
progression.nextLesson: how controlling mosquitoes can stop disease spreading (route entry bio-m7-b12).

teaching.task: Three antibiotic discs on one plate: one clears a big zone, one a small zone, one nothing. Is the biggest zone the best medicine, and is the third drug useless? How do you run a safe, fair disc test, and what can its zones really tell you?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) the puzzle; (2) a disc's drug diffuses out, so it is strongest near the disc; where it is strong enough the bacteria can't grow, giving a clear zone; beyond the edge it is too dilute (the zone's edge is where the drug just stops growth); (3) aim and variables; (4) the blank control shows the disc and water alone don't stop growth; three plates with rotated positions so one plate or spot can't decide it; (5) a lawn needs an even spread; discs spaced so zones don't overlap, pressed to touch the agar so the drug can diffuse; (6) tape, invert, 25 to 30 °C, never opened (recall); (7) measure through the base, twice at right angles; no zone recorded as 6 mm; (8) results, means, reliability, the blank's meaning; (9) zone size also depends on dose and diffusion, and on whether the bacterium has the target; (10) a plate is not a patient; the narrow conclusion; (11) VRA; (12) risk; attempts; decision rule and handoff; key notes.
teaching.conversationalApproach: a student puts discs on a plate of bacteria and two days later disc A has a 25 millimetre clear zone, B 15 and C nothing, so the practical asks whether A is the best medicine and C useless, and what a zone of inhibition can and can't show. Each disc holds a measured dose that diffuses outwards, strongest near the disc, and where it is strong enough to stop growth the agar stays clear: the zone of inhibition. The aim compares three antibiotic discs on one harmless bacterium, with the antibiotic as the independent variable, zone diameter as the dependent variable and everything else kept the same, plus a sterile-water blank disc as the negative control and three plates with the discs in different positions. The teacher supplies an approved culture spread as a lawn, discs go on with sterile forceps well apart, and the plate is closed, labelled, inverted and incubated at 25 to 30 degrees, never 37, with the lid kept shut and zones measured through the base. The results show A larger than B with close repeats and no zone for the blank, but zone size also depends on dose and on how far the drug diffuses, and a plate isn't a patient, so the claim stays narrow. Validity, reliability and accuracy each get their plain question, and the risk assessment keeps cultured plates closed. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: A student put four paper discs on a plate spread with bacteria. Two days later, around disc A, a clear zone twenty five millimetres across. Around disc B, fifteen. Around disc C, nothing. So is A the best medicine, and is C useless? The plate can't tell you either.
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1, assess, 3 marks) Discs P and Q (6 mm), a harmless bacterium, 48 h at 28 °C; mean zones P 22 mm, Q 13 mm, sterile water disc 6 mm; her conclusion "P would be the more effective treatment for an infection in people". Answer: judgement (only partly supported, or not supported as a treatment claim); evidence (P's 22 mm against Q's 13 mm and the 6 mm control: P produced a larger clear zone than Q under these conditions, and the paper and water alone produced none); reason the claim overreaches (zone size also depends on dose and diffusion; treatment depends on reaching the infection safely and on the actual pathogen, shown by clinical trials). Crossed mistake: "biggest zone = best medicine". (A2, identify and propose, 4 marks) Antiseptic X disc soaked 1 min, antiseptic Y disc soaked 10 min, one plate, 37 °C, lid removed to measure. Answer: any two problems with a fix that removes each: unequal soaking (equal time, or the same measured volume on each disc); lid removed (keep taped, measure through the base); 37 °C (25 to 30 °C); one plate and no control (three plates, a blank disc dipped in sterile water). Feedback voices soaking and the lid, names the other two in one sentence. Crossed mistake: "be more careful when opening the lid" (the plate should not be opened at all; the fix does not remove the exposure). Antiseptics are used in A2 (not antibiotics) so the item is unseen in substance as well as numbers; the method skills are the same. The card says "antiseptic solutions", so no pharmaceutical claim is made.
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Biology Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "investigate and assess the effectiveness of pharmaceuticals as treatment strategies for the control of infectious disease, for example:; antivirals; antibiotics" this video prepares students to plan, run and interpret a disc-diffusion test; watching it is not doing it. It teaches: what a zone of inhibition is and why it forms (the drug diffuses out and thins with distance); the aim and variables; the negative control and three plates; preparing a lawn of a supplied harmless culture; placing and spacing discs; closing the lid as the school procedure directs, inverting and incubating at 25 to 30 °C (recalled from p02 in one sentence); measuring the zone through the base, twice at right angles; reading the results table and means; what zone size depends on besides how active the drug is (dose, diffusion, whether the bacterium has the drug's target); why a plate is not a patient (reaching the infection, safety, the actual pathogen, clinical trials); validity, reliability and accuracy; the risk assessment (contamination, closed plates, antibiotic allergy, autoclaving). Not re-taught: selective toxicity and drug targets (b11; one clause in scene 9, "the part C targets"); clinical trials as evidence (b11 scene 10; one clause in scene 10); serial dilution, aseptic technique, labelling, taping and inverting, and 25 to 30 °C (p02; one sentence in scene 6, one gloss in scene 5); resistance by selection (b11; a silent tag in scene 8). Not here: standardised clinical susceptibility testing (Mueller-Hinton agar, McFarland standard, breakpoint tables: author note only, one grey tag in scene 9); antivirals (they cannot be tested on bacterial agar; one grey tag in scene 2, as b11 taught); minimum inhibitory concentration; resistance mechanisms (b11).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key: the antibiotic violet (the independent variable); zone diameters amber (the dependent variable); the control green; "on this plate" teal and "as a medicine" terracotta, kept apart wherever both appear; hazards terracotta; grey for tags and callbacks. Clutter rule: at most three bright text items; every tag dims when its sentence ends. All incubated plates on screen are lidded and taped; no lid lifts after incubation, ever. Reuse: the explainer kit (`Plate`, `Callout`, `Mark`, `Countdown`, `HandText`, `DrawPath`, `scribbleEllipse`, `Enter`); B6a's `WrongChip`, `GreyTag`, `Cross`, `Cam`; bio-m7-p02's step rail, variables card, VRA cards, risk table and claim card (lesson-local there; root to decide copy or lift, as p02's open decision). New coded items (lesson-local): the diffusion halo (a coded radial gradient of small amber dots, dense at the disc and thinning outward, with a dashed ring at the "just enough to stop growth" level, laid over the painted zones plate), the ruler readout (coded mm numerals and two perpendicular measurement lines over the painted ruler; numerals only, no coded ruler body), the zone table (four rows, three plates and a mean), and the depends-on fan (four short spokes from a zone thumbnail: "how active the drug is", "dose in disc", "how far it diffuses", "target present?"). No human figures.
